segments.text: Forensic psychology applies psychological knowledge to legal and criminal-justice settings. It may involve investigation, memory, confession, assessment, offender work and court-related questions.
This unit should be handled carefully. Psychology can inform legal processes, but it does not provide a magical “lie detector” or allow certain predictions about guilt from body language.

items.text: Psychology and law

: Psychology contributes research and professional expertise to legal questions, while legal standards determine what is admissible or legally relevant. The two fields use different concepts and goals.
Investigation
: Psychological research can inform interviewing, decision making, memory retrieval and investigative practice. Good interviewing avoids unnecessarily suggestive questions.
Confession

: Confessions can be influenced by interrogation conditions, vulnerability, fatigue, pressure and expectations. A confession should not automatically be treated as error-proof simply because it was made.
Eyewitness testimony
: Memory is reconstructive. Stress, attention, delay, suggestion, lineup procedure and post-event information can affect eyewitness accuracy and confidence.
Working with offenders
: Forensic work may involve assessment of needs, risk factors, treatment targets and rehabilitation. Ethical practice requires validated methods and awareness of limits.
Juvenile delinquency

: Young offenders differ developmentally from adults. Family, peers, schooling, neighbourhood, substance use and individual factors can interact; simplistic single-cause explanations should be avoided.
Drug addiction and sex offenders
: These groups require evidence-based assessment and intervention. Avoid stereotypes: not every person with substance-use problems or a particular history has the same risk profile.

blocks.text: The boundary between psychology and law

segments.text: Forensic psychology applies psychological science and professional practice to legal questions. Courts decide legal standards such as guilt, admissibility and responsibility; psychologists provide evidence about memory, assessment, development, behaviour and risk within the limits of their expertise. Confusing these roles leads to overclaiming.

items.text: Investigative versus clinical roles

: An investigative consultant may advise on interviewing or decision processes, while a forensic clinician may conduct an assessment for a legal purpose. Therapeutic confidentiality and forensic disclosure obligations can differ substantially.
Evidence versus intuition
: Body language, handwriting or a supposed 'criminal personality' cannot reliably determine guilt. Forensic conclusions should rely on validated methods and converging evidence.
Encoding conditions
: Attention, lighting, duration, distance, stress and weapon focus can affect what information is encoded during an event.
Retention interval
: Memory changes over time, and later information can become integrated with the original memory.
Suggestive questioning
: Loftus and Palmer's 1974 research showed that wording of post-event questions can influence later reports. The broader lesson is that memory is reconstructive and interview procedures matter.
Lineups

: Fair lineup composition and instructions reduce the risk that a witness chooses the person who merely looks most like the remembered offender. Confidence is informative only under appropriate testing conditions and should not be treated as a simple guarantee of accuracy.
Open prompts
: Information-gathering interviews generally begin with open invitations and use non-leading follow-up questions. This reduces contamination and can produce fuller accounts.
Coercive pressure
: Lengthy questioning, sleep deprivation, threats, false evidence ploys and vulnerability can increase risk of unreliable confession in some circumstances.
Individual vulnerability
: Young age, intellectual limitations, mental health problems and suggestibility can affect understanding and resistance to pressure. Safeguards should therefore be adapted to vulnerability.
Corroboration
: A confession should be checked against independent facts. Details first supplied by investigators rather than the suspect should not be misinterpreted as independent knowledge.
Risk factors

: Risk assessment identifies factors statistically or clinically associated with future offending. It estimates probability under specified conditions; it does not predict an individual's future with certainty.
Static and dynamic factors

: Static factors such as past history cannot be changed, while dynamic factors such as substance misuse, attitudes or social circumstances may become treatment targets. Distinguishing them connects assessment with intervention.
Structured approaches
: Validated actuarial or structured professional judgment tools can improve consistency over unstructured intuition, but they still require appropriate populations and transparent limitations.
Rehabilitation

: Evidence-based rehabilitation often focuses on criminogenic needs, skills, substance problems, education, relationships and reintegration. Punishment alone does not explain how future offending risk changes.
Development

: Adolescents differ from adults in impulse control, reward sensitivity, peer influence and long-term planning. Developmental evidence supports age-appropriate justice responses without implying that every young offender is the same.
Substance-use problems

: Addiction is associated with learning, reward systems, stress, social context and availability. Forensic assessment should distinguish substance dependence, intoxication, withdrawal and offending context rather than treating drug use as a single personality type.
Sexual offending

: Risk and treatment vary across individuals and offence patterns. Stereotypes are poor substitutes for structured assessment, and ethical practice requires careful language, validated tools and attention to public safety.
Ethics

: Forensic psychologists must explain role, limits of confidentiality, purpose of assessment and potential recipients of the report. Objectivity is especially important because the evaluator may be retained by one side but owes professional duties to the integrity of the assessment.

items.text: Learn one page on eyewitness memory and one on confession because both allow strong analytical answers.
Use “risk factors” rather than claiming certainty about future offending.
Distinguish investigative interviewing from coercive interrogation.
Add ethics and limitations to assessment questions.

rows: Avoid this error Do not claim that psychologists can identify guilt accurately from facial expressions, handwriting or “criminal personality” alone.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Define forensic psychology, explain its relationship with law, then cover investigation/confession, eyewitness testimony, offender work and special populations, ending with ethics and limitations.
• Loftus & Palmer (1974), Reconstruction of Automobile Destruction; contemporary eyewitness and confession research should be interpreted with procedural context.
• Memory is reconstructive, so eyewitness evidence can be affected by conditions.
• A confession is important evidence but can still be unreliable under some circumstances.
• Forensic assessment must use evidence-based tools and clear limits.
• Legal conclusions and psychological findings are related but not identical.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
